items.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: I always heard traditional music... I mean I always heard... Clifford Brown quite naturally... Clifford Brown used to wear that thing out... Clifford Brown displayed... how to play melody.

ctx.x: Did he continue to play in New Orleans some?

Yeah he played a lot with like Paul Barbarin, Uncle Lester Santiago played piano in the band, and when my dad first came back, my uncle was like, “Man you’d better learn to play some of this music.” And my dad wasn’t playing traditional music at all. So he and my uncle Lester used to practice together. They lived on Villere Street in the Tremaine. That’s where my uncle used to live. And my dad said he would go over there just about every day, they’d go over a few songs and that’s how he met my mom, practicing…

items.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I heard great music growing up... Clifford Brown, Dizzy Gillespie... my brother was born of that generation. So I heard great music growing up.

ctx.x: So in other words a song, a real song, doesn’t just come because you know the notes and the scales and you can play chord X. Songs come from experience. Talk to us about real experience.

Well experience and emotion. Emotion is one of the main like parts of playing a song. Especially a ballad. You have to really know the words basically to the ballad. And the words, I try to make that come out of the end of the horn. One of my favorite records, you know when Dan was saying about Louis Armstrong, he’s number one. Whoever doesn’t think Louis Armstrong is number one has the wrong idea. I’m very convinced of that. Because without Louis Armstrong, I don’t know where jazz would be. I don’t know, I…

Talk to us about, I caught a couple of your sets, which were just beautiful. Talk to us about your tone and some of your influences on the trumpet. You’ve already talked about Louis. But who did you listen to to help you formulate your tone and the way you play? Because the way you play is quite distinctive.
